name: Delhi/NCR
unit_type: City (NCT of Delhi) within a multi-state regional airshed
selection_category: Anchor: urban and regional pollution, outdoor work, restrictions
why_chosen: Most-studied Indian setting; the only one with a statutory regional commission (CAQM), a graded emergency plan (GRAP) that stops work, and court-ordered worker compensation. It shows both the harm and the side-effects of emergency control.
pollution_exposure_profile: Winter PM2.5 at sampling sites averaged 168 µg/m³ (2016-17); secondary particles and biomass burning rise in winter, dust dominates in summer. Local sources were about 35% of PM2.5 in the November 2025 episode window, with vehicles about half of the local share. The AQI cap (500) and exclusion of readings above 999 µg/m³ hide the worst hours.
communities_livelihoods: Construction workers (largely migrant), street vendors, waste pickers, sanitation workers, delivery riders, auto drivers, homeless people, residents of informal settlements and resettlement colonies.
health_livelihood_evidence: Moderate for exposure and health association (sampling studies, occupational spirometry, ten-city mortality). Limited for earnings: compensation records and small surveys, no measured income-loss study for vendors or gig workers found.
existing_responses: GRAP restrictions; Supreme Court-mandated compensation via the BOCW Welfare Board; NCAP grants; school closure protocols; DUSIB winter shelters; smog towers and anti-smog guns (evaluated as ineffective or unproven); NGO organising (MHT, Chintan, Help Delhi Breathe).
gaps: Registration gap blocks compensation; no protection for non-construction outdoor workers during restrictions; earnings losses unmeasured; NCAP funds under-used (17% by Dec 2025 per CSE).
illustrates_beyond_delhi: Baseline case: shows how emergency controls create a policy-mediated livelihood pathway distinct from illness.
cannot_generalise: Delhi's source shares, institutional capacity, court oversight and media attention are not typical; GRAP and compensation exist only in NCR.

name: Bihar: Patna and rural Bihar
unit_type: State-level region of the Indo-Gangetic Plain; one city (Patna) plus rural blocks
selection_category: Another IGP city/district; smaller cities and rural areas with limited monitoring; rural household energy
why_chosen: Persistent regional exposure with far lower monitoring and institutional capacity than Delhi; household biomass and kilns matter more; illustrates exposure in places that official networks barely see.
pollution_exposure_profile: Low-cost sensors in every block of 38 districts recorded violations of the national standard on nearly 90% of days, with winter PM2.5 around 210 µg/m³ in the north-west. In Patna, residential (household) sources were modelled at 28% of winter PM2.5 and dust dominated PM10.
communities_livelihoods: Rural households cooking with biomass (women and children most exposed), brick-kiln workers, agricultural workers, migrants (Bihar is a major origin state for kiln and construction migrants).
health_livelihood_evidence: Limited: sensor data disputed by the state board; birth-outcome studies show steeper risk in northern districts but no Bihar-specific livelihood evidence found.
existing_responses: BSPCB kiln conversion notification (March 2022); Patna source apportionment (TERI, Bloomberg-supported); IIT Kanpur AMRIT sensor network; planned studies in Gaya and Muzaffarpur; PMUY LPG connections with low refill rates.
gaps: Roughly one regulatory monitor per 3.5-4 million people; no health or earnings data at block level; dispute over data credibility.
illustrates_beyond_delhi: Shows that pollution is a rural and regional problem, not just a metropolitan one, and that monitoring gaps hide it.
cannot_generalise: Sensor readings are not regulatory-grade; Patna shares cannot be transferred to rural blocks.

name: Singrauli coal and power belt (Madhya Pradesh / Uttar Pradesh border)
unit_type: Industrial and mining cluster spanning two states
selection_category: Industrial or mining belt: occupational, community and ambient exposure
why_chosen: Concentration of coal mines and thermal power plants; tests whether community exposure near large formal industry differs from urban mixed sources.
pollution_exposure_profile: Annual PM10 of about 160-167 µg/m³ at two official stations (2023-24) against a 60 µg/m³ standard; PM2.5 not reported there; black carbon above 200 µg/m³ near plants in a short 2013 campaign; persistent satellite NO2 hotspot.
communities_livelihoods: Mine and plant workers, contract labour, displaced and resettled communities, residents near ash ponds and coal transport routes.
health_livelihood_evidence: Limited: allegations of respiratory harm and heavy-metal exposure before the NGT are unadjudicated; official health data are sparse.
existing_responses: CEPI action plan (critically polluted area); NGT proceedings (OA 240/2024); industrial emission norms and FGD requirements.
gaps: No independent community health study found; PM2.5 not monitored at key stations; legal process rather than services is the main route for residents.
illustrates_beyond_delhi: Formal industry with identifiable polluters: accountability can run through regulation and litigation rather than informal-sector support.
cannot_generalise: Findings near coal plants do not transfer to cities dominated by traffic or dust.

name: Mumbai
selection_category: Western/southern metro: transport, construction, industry, informal employment
why_chosen: Large coastal metro where sea breezes once implied cleaner air; construction boom and informal industry; tests transfer of Delhi framings to a different airshed.
pollution_exposure_profile: Road dust is the main PM10 source; secondary aerosols (22%) and marine sources (26%) make up about half of PM2.5. Receptor modelling attributes 12-20% to industry but the inventory under 1%, because informal furnaces (bhatties) are not inventoried.
communities_livelihoods: Construction workers (Metro and real estate), informal industrial workers, street vendors, residents of informal settlements near roads and waste sites.
health_livelihood_evidence: Limited for health and livelihoods specific to Mumbai in this review.
existing_responses: BMC construction-site guidelines (October 2023 onward); MPCB source apportionment and emission inventory (NEERI, December 2023).
gaps: No worker-focused exposure or earnings evidence found; informal sources missing from inventories.
illustrates_beyond_delhi: Different airshed and source mix; shows that inventories miss informal sources, so plans built on them can miss what workers breathe.
cannot_generalise: Marine contribution and meteorology are specific to the coast.

name: Rural Punjab and Haryana (paddy residue belt)
selection_category: Rural agricultural setting with seasonal burning
why_chosen: Origin of the most politically visible seasonal source; tests who pays for transition (farmers, labourers) and what rural residents themselves breathe.
pollution_exposure_profile: Short, intense burning seasons; one village study recorded a mean PM2.5 increase of 167 µg/m³ during burning. Satellite fire counts fell sharply: Punjab 5,114 in 2025, down 93% on 2021.
communities_livelihoods: Small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, rural children and older adults.
health_livelihood_evidence: Moderate for acute respiratory effect in villages (lung function falls during burning, largest among 10-18-year-olds); no adequate evidence found on farmer or labourer earnings effects of residue rules.
existing_responses: Central crop-residue machinery subsidies (about ₹3,623 crore released FY2018-19 to FY2024-25 to four states); enforcement squads; ex-situ straw use; World Bank programme in Haryana.
gaps: Distribution of transition costs across farm sizes and labourers is unmeasured; satellite counts may miss small or late fires.
illustrates_beyond_delhi: Rural exposure from agricultural sources affects the source communities themselves, not only Delhi.
cannot_generalise: Season-specific and crop-specific; not a model for year-round urban pollution.

name: Brick-kiln clusters (Bihar and Punjab examples)
unit_type: Dispersed peri-urban and rural production clusters (occupational setting)
why_chosen: Labour-intensive, seasonal, coal-fired production with migrant family labour; the clearest case of cleaner production meeting precarious work.
pollution_exposure_profile: Kilns contribute locally (about 10-11% of winter PM in Patna attributed to industry/brick kilns); workers are exposed to coal dust and heat on site and live in temporary housing.
communities_livelihoods: Seasonal migrant families paid as units by piece rate, disproportionately Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe; children often present and working.
health_livelihood_evidence: Moderate for labour conditions (debt bondage, withheld wages) from advocacy surveys; Limited for health; no adequate evidence found on how zigzag conversion changed workers' pay, debt or exposure.
existing_responses: Zigzag conversion directives (CPCB 2015; BSPCB 2022); WRI India and partners' training modules for masons.
gaps: Worker outcomes of conversion unmeasured; no official count of kilns or workers.
illustrates_beyond_delhi: Cleaner technology can reduce emissions while leaving bonded labour and exposure untouched.
cannot_generalise: Kiln labour regimes vary by state; Punjab survey is older (c.2017).
